content.prompt: Use a stream to filter this list to only even numbers and collect into a new list.

content.text: An Iterator is a bookmark in a book — it tracks your position and lets you move forward one page at a time (and optionally rip out the current page safely). A Stream is a conveyor belt in a factory: items flow through stations (filter, transform, collect) and you get the finished product at the end without touching the original pile.

content.annotation: filter() keeps elements matching a condition. map() transforms each element. collect() gathers results into a new collection. The original list is NEVER modified — streams are non-mutating pipelines. A stream can only be consumed ONCE — after a terminal operation (forEach, collect), it is closed. Reusing a consumed stream throws IllegalStateException. The for-each loop uses an Iterator internally; calling list.remove() directly during iteration causes ConcurrentModificationException because the Iterator's modification count becomes out of sync. Use Iterator.remove() to safely remove during iteration.

content.modification: We call forEach() on the same stream TWICE.
content.question: What happens on the second forEach()?
content.explanation: A stream can only be consumed ONCE. After a terminal operation like forEach or collect, the stream is closed. Reusing a consumed stream throws IllegalStateException. Create a new stream from the source to process again.

content.label: Traditional loop vs Stream pipeline
content.question: What's the main advantage of the stream approach?
options: Reads like a description of intent
content.explanation: A stream is a conveyor belt — items flow through stations (filter, transform, collect) describing WHAT you want, not HOW. The original list is never modified. Streams are non-mutating pipelines that read like a description of intent rather than step-by-step instructions.
